rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states that the technical documentation must include 'a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run', citing Annex IV point 1(e), which conveys the substance of the requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 contains no "medium-risk" grade, and on these facts the AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1): it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (medical devices, Annex I, point 11), and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market under that legislation. Both conditions in Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are met, so the MDR's own "medium-risk" (e.g. Class IIa/IIb) grading does not transfer to the AI system, it only triggers the notified-body condition. The derogation in Article 6(3) is irrelevant, as it applies only to the Annex III listed-use route. Consequences: the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply and are assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure as a single assessment (Article 43(3)), with points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also applying. Article 8 lets the provider integrate that testing, reporting and documentation into the existing MDR procedures to avoid duplication.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the EU AI Act has no 'medium-risk' category and explicitly affirms the AI system is high-risk.
The answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745), satisfying condition (a).
The answer confirms the product undergoes third-party conformity assessment under the applicable legislation, satisfying condition (b).

The answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and that the sectoral risk classification (e.g., 'medium-risk') does not apply to the AI system's risk classification under the AI Act.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with no self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically ordered and actionable for a compliance professional.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and no, it is not high-risk on the biometrics route. None of the prohibited practices in Article 5(1) covers it, in particular it is neither a biometric categorisation system inferring sensitive attributes under Article 5(1)(g) nor real-time remote biometric identification. Annex III, point 1(a) expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be, so it is not high-risk under Article 6(2). It could still be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of an Annex I product.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the system is not prohibited, aligning with the correct verdict.
The answer clearly states the system is not high-risk under the biometrics route and explains it is excluded from Annex III.1(a), which suffices for the 'not high-risk' verdict in this context.
The answer cites the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems with the specified sole purpose, stating the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs human oversight. It requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use (Article 14(1)), with oversight measures commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use (Article 14(3)).
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight.
The answer cites Article 14(1), which requires design for effective human oversight during use.
The answer does not mention that human oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights.

The answer refers to oversight measures being commensurate with risks and context, and implies provider responsibility through design, aligning with measures built in by the provider; it does not explicitly mention deployer implementation, but 'measures commensurate' contextually includes both where appropriate.
The answer does not state that overseers must be enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, or halt the system; these specific capabilities are omitted.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; uses precise regulatory language without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer affirms the existence of exceptions in Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly states that (c) and (d) still apply.
The answer states the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices laid down in Article 5 attracts the Regulation's highest penalty tier: administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). The ceiling applies to breach of any of the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), points (a) to (h), whether committed by a provider, deployer or other operator placing on the market, putting into service or using such a system. Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, each fine ceiling applies up to the percentage or the fixed amount referred to, whichever is lower (Article 99(6)). Fines must in every case be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and set with regard to the gravity and nature of the infringement (Article 99(1) and (7)). Article 5 breaches are expressly carved out of the lower EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % tier in Article 99(4).
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the fine amount and turnover percentage, specifying 'whichever is higher' as required.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fines to non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices in Article 5, including reference to Article 5(1) points (a) to (h).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is in neutral, professional language, directly quoting the definition from the Act in a clear and concise manner suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases), capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems carry transparency duties under Article 50, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer notes that minimal-risk systems avoid high-risk obligations and mentions voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95, thereby stating the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose suitable for regulatory advice; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming the possibility.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market results in being considered a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering condition.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The objective of the Regulation, stated in Article 1(1), is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. To that end, Article 1(2) lays down the harmonised rules giving effect to that purpose.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the objective includes improving the functioning of the internal market.
The answer explicitly states the promotion of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer includes the full scope of protection: health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection against harmful effects of AI.
The answer explicitly mentions supporting innovation as part of the objective.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents the information in clear, coherent prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as the initial verdict, which matches the required 'No' in criterion 1 and is unambiguous.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and cites the correct provision, Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly excludes profiling of natural persons from the derogation by stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which captures the exception in the criterion.
The answer references Article 6(4) and states the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, which matches the requirement in the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 101, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed (Article 101(5)). That unlimited jurisdiction goes beyond ordinary legality review: the Court may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, in either direction, so a provider bringing an action risks an increase as well as a reduction or annulment of the fine. The fines subject to this review are those the Commission may impose under Article 101(1), not exceeding 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, fixed having regard to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and the principles of proportionality and appropriateness, and which must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(1), (3)).
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel, reduce or increase the fine,' including 'cancel' as required by criterion 2.
The answer includes 'reduce the fine' as one of the Court's powers, satisfying criterion 3.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may...increase the fine,' satisfying criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, coherent structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Before placing a high-risk Annex III system on the market or putting it into service, the provider (or authorised representative) must register itself and the system in the EU database, entering the data listed in Section A of Annex VIII (Article 49(1); Article 71(2)). Those items are: the provider's name, address and contact details; where another person submits on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the authorised representative's name, address and contact details, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing its identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported through the system; a basic and concise description of the information used (data, inputs) and the operating logic; the system's status (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market/in service, recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the notified body's certificate and that body's name or identification number, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; the Member States where the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use, except for law enforcement and migration, asylum and border-control systems under Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7; and, optionally, a URL for additional information (Annex VIII, points 1 to 13). Where the provider concludes under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, the same registration duty applies to that system and its documented self-assessment (Article 49(2); Article 6(4)), and for systems in the law enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control areas of Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7, registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database limited to the reduced set of items in Article 49(4).
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer includes the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable.
The answer states the requirement for the AI system's trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability.
The answer includes a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported by the system.
The answer provides a basic and concise description of the data, inputs, and operating logic.
The answer covers the system's status and the notified body certificate details including type, number, expiry date, body identification, and scanned copy where applicable.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use, noting the exception for certain Annex III systems.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The answer states the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: Answer states processing is allowed only when strictly necessary and cannot be effectively fulfilled with other data, including synthetic or anonymised.
Answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
Answer covers strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and prohibits transmission or access by others.
Answer explicitly states deletion upon bias correction or end of retention period, whichever comes first.
Answer notes that records must document the necessity and why other data types would not suffice.
Answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear, coherent prose suitable for regulatory use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the instructions for use accompanying a high-risk AI system must be concise, complete, correct and clear, and contain six categories of information. The identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative. The characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including intended purpose, the levels of accuracy (with metrics), robustness and cybersecurity against which the system was tested and validated, known or foreseeable circumstances affecting those levels, performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which it is intended to be used, specifications for input data, and information enabling deployers to interpret the output. Changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the initial conformity assessment. The human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs. The computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and necessary maintenance and care measures, including their frequency and software updates. Where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12.
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the requirement to include the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, the authorised representative.

The answer lists all required sub-elements under characteristics, capabilities and limitations, including intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity with metrics, foreseeable risks, performance for specific groups, input data specifications, and information to interpret outputs.
The answer includes pre-determined changes to the system and its performance as required.
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs.
The answer covers computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance measures including frequency and software updates.
The answer includes, where relevant, a description of mechanisms for log collection, storage and interpretation in accordance with Article 12.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, and may cover one or more AI systems taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems (Article 95(3)). The bodies that must encourage and facilitate their drawing up are the AI Office and the Member States: under Article 95(1) they shall encourage and facilitate codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, fostering voluntary application to non-high-risk AI systems of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Under Article 95(2) they shall also facilitate codes covering voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators. Under Article 95(4) they shall take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The answer states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly mentions involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

The answer clearly identifies the AI Office and the Member States as the bodies required to encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, citing both Article 95(1) and (2), satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner as written policies, procedures and instructions, and including at least the following thirteen aspects. (a) A strategy for regulatory compliance, covering conformity assessment procedures and management of modifications to the system. (b) Techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification. (c) Techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance. (d) Examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and their frequency. (e) Technical specifications, including standards, and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, the means used to ensure compliance. (f) Systems and procedures for data management, including acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention. (g) The risk management system referred to in Article 9. (h) Setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72. (i) Procedures for reporting serious incidents under Article 73. (j) Handling of communication with national competent and other authorities, notified bodies, other operators, customers and interested parties. (k) Systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information. (l) Resource management, including security-of-supply measures. (m) An accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff for all those aspects. Implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation while respecting the required rigour and level of protection (Article 17(2)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) unless and in so far as it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives. First, the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)). Second, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)). Third, the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Use is confined to confirming the identity of the specifically targeted individual (Article 5(2)).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, matching the substance of criterion 1.

The candidate answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety and the prevention of a genuine terrorist attack, covering the substance of criterion 2.

The candidate answer correctly identifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for serious offences listed in Annex II punishable by at least four years’ imprisonment, aligning with the substance of criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise references; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated; the technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking account of the specificities and limitations of content types, implementation costs and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as reflected in relevant technical standards. This does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(2)).

Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated

Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer explicitly requires that outputs be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer includes the requirement for technical solutions to be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer references that feasibility is assessed considering content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and the state of the art.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing functions, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, and law enforcement authorisation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, i.e. the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and it must entrust the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). National market surveillance authorities have no enforcement competence over Chapter V; they may only request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where necessary and proportionate to assist them in fulfilling their own tasks, without prejudice to Article 75(3) (Article 88(2)). Consistently with that allocation, providers of general-purpose AI models must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities (Article 53(3)), and providers of models with systemic risk report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office (Article 55(1)(c)). The evidence supplied contains no text for Articles 25, 41 or 56, so no finding is made on those.
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V.
The candidate answer clearly states that the Commission entrusts the implementation of these tasks to the AI Office.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory information.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing high-risk AI systems in real world conditions may be transferred to a third country only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). This is not a stand‑alone permission but one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4): the transfer safeguard must be satisfied alongside every other condition in that paragraph, so a transfer is lawful only while the testing itself remains lawful. The "safeguards under Union law" referred to are those of Union data protection law governing transfers to third countries, together with any stricter protection attaching to special categories of personal data; the AI Act itself adds no separate adequacy or authorisation mechanism. Where the safeguards cannot be implemented, the data must remain within the Union, and subjects retain their right to request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data (Article 60(5)).
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by explicitly requiring that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law be implemented for the transfer.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the two conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Article 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model shall be classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions, so satisfying one suffices. Under Article 51(1)(a), the model has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; "high-impact capabilities" means capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)). Under Article 51(1)(b), the classification follows from a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption, not a third condition: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under point (a) where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, specifying it as a rebuttable presumption under Article 51(2) and linking it to high-impact capabilities.

The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, either ex officio or following a qualified alert, based on equivalence to high-impact capabilities using Annex XIII criteria, is sufficient for classification.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives and that satisfying one suffices, directly matching the 'no' verdict in the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and precise references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Classification under Article 6(1) requires both conditions to be met cumulatively: under Article 6(1), point (a), the AI system must be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in satisfied here, since Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is listed in Annex I. But under Article 6(1), point (b), that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market; a non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable-surgical Class I device is self-certified without a notified body, so point (b) fails. The system would still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it falls within a use case listed in Annex III.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the initial and unambiguous position.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions under Article 6(1) must be met cumulatively.
The answer correctly explains that Class I devices of this type are self-certified and do not require third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that because point (b) fails, the Article 6(1) high-risk classification does not apply, which directly satisfies the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift can qualify as a high-risk AI system, and it does so under the product route in Article 6(1) rather than under the Annex III listed-use route. Two cumulative conditions must be fulfilled. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts is listed in Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift (or the safety component itself as a product) must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. Classification applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Where both conditions are met, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under Directive 2014/33/EU, into which the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements are integrated (Article 43(3)).
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its opening word, making the affirmative position unambiguous.

The answer states that the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifically cites Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts as being in Annex I, point 4.
The answer clearly states that the lift (or the AI system as a product) must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the relevant Directive.
The answer explicitly describes the two conditions as 'cumulative' and states that classification applies only 'where both conditions are met'.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, professional, and uses the precise regulatory language without any self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both, and both immediately, the duties are cumulative, not alternatives, and neither waits on the authority. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the Article 44 certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2) is additional, not a substitute: operators must cooperate, and where non-compliance is found the authority requires corrective action, withdrawal or recall within a prescribed period. Article 79(4) obliges the operator to extend corrective action to all systems concerned; failure triggers provisional measures under Article 79(5).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties apply and are cumulative, satisfying the 'Both' criterion.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's obligation to immediately take corrective action upon awareness of non-compliance.
The answer clearly states that under Article 20(2), the provider must immediately investigate the causes, establishing it as a direct duty.
The answer specifies that investigation must be done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and does not defer to the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate; the duty is real. Article 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the Section 2 requirements. The "where applicable" wording covers systems supplied on physical media or embedded in products, where handling can degrade conformity; purely online delivery simply makes the condition inapplicable.

Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: No, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 neither prohibits drones nor lists them as such; the classification follows the AI system's intended purpose, not the airframe. Using a drone's AI to identify who is around town engages Article 5(1)(h)'s prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces where done for law enforcement, and otherwise falls under Annex III, point 1 as high-risk remote biometric identification; mere detection of persons without biometric identification does not. A toy drone falls under Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I, point 2), so its AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) only where the toy must undergo third-party conformity assessment; toy drones in other applications are tested by the same purpose-based route.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on the AI system's intended use, not the drone itself, aligning with Article 6.

Correctly identifies that using AI in a drone to identify people in public constitutes remote biometric identification, which is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), and distinguishes it from the 1:1 verification exclusion.
Explains that toy status does not exempt the AI system from high-risk classification if the intended use meets criteria under Article 6(1) or Annex III.
Clarifies that a toy drone used for other applications is assessed based on its intended purpose and may be high-risk only if it falls under Annex III or Article 6(1) conditions.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed. As deployer the operator must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the system is used in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)); a use outside the intended purpose breaches that duty irrespective of the operator's legal team's risk view. The operator's legal team's conclusion also misreads the test. The system's high-risk status attaches under Article 6(1) (Annex I product route) or Article 6(2) (Annex III listed use-cases) as placed on the market; a new off-label application does not declassify it. The Article 6(3) derogation is available only for Annex III systems meeting one of the four conditions (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task), never where profiling of natural persons occurs, and it is a provider self-assessment documented before placing on the market, not a deployer judgement afterwards. If you modify the intended purpose or make a substantial modification, the operator is considered a provider and assume the Article 16 provider obligations (Article 25(1)). Yes, keep logs: automatically generated logs under the operator's control must be retained at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)), alongside the Article 26(5) monitoring and serious-incident notification duty.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply proceed,' which matches the required verdict.
The answer explicitly references Article 26(1) and explains that use must be in accordance with instructions for use, and that deviation is not permitted even if the new use is deemed low-risk.
The answer affirms the logging obligation under Article 26(6), stating logs must be kept for at least six months if under the deployer's control, regardless of the specific use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, potentially. Software that supports clinicians in choosing treatment is normally a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, which appears in Annex I, Section A, point 11; it is therefore high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is the product, or a safety component of a product, covered by that legislation and requires third‑party conformity assessment thereunder. Annex III does not list clinical treatment decision‑making.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

The answer cites Article 6(1) as the applicable provision, not Article 6(2), and explicitly distinguishes the basis of classification under 6(1) from Annex III, thereby failing to state the substance of criterion 2.

The answer explicitly states that 'Annex III does not list clinical treatment decision-making', which contradicts the required substance that the system falls under Annex III (healthcare access/provision); thus, it fails to satisfy the criterion.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four; no to the fifth. Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII, the information made available to providers intending to integrate the model must include its date of release and methods of distribution, its architecture and number of parameters, how the model interacts with hardware or software external to it where applicable, and the licence. Samples of outlier training data are not required, only a description of the training data, including type and provenance.

The answer explicitly lists the license as required information, satisfying the criterion.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not one of the high-risk areas; Annex III lists eight areas and clinical decision-making is not among them. The eight areas under Annex III are: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Under Article 6(2) a system is high-risk only if it falls within a lettered use-case under one of those areas, not merely within the subject-matter of the area. Healthcare enters only through specific listed use-cases in Annex III(5): point (a), evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them; point (c), risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance; and point (d), emergency call triage and dispatch, including emergency healthcare patient triage. Separately, clinical software may be high-risk by the Annex I route under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is, a medical device requiring third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer lists all eight areas specified in Annex III, using substantively equivalent terms.

The candidate answer clearly states that healthcare decision making is not one of the high-risk areas, which aligns with the criterion's 'No' verdict, and explains why by distinguishing general clinical decision-making from the specific healthcare-related use cases actually listed in Annex III.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No, introducing guardrails cannot move a system from high-risk to a lower tier. Classification under Article 6(1), (2) turns on the Annex I product route or the Annex III listed use-case, not on mitigation; Article 8(1) confirms the Section 2 requirements apply taking the intended purpose and the Article 9 risk-management system into account, so guardrails are the means of compliance, not an exit from it. Changing capabilities and intended use can change classification: if the redefined purpose falls outside any Annex III use-case, or within the Article 6(3) derogation (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task, never where it profiles natural persons), with the self-assessment documented beforehand. But under Article 25(1)(b), (c), a substantial modification that keeps the system high-risk, or a modification of intended purpose that makes a non-high-risk system high-risk, makes the modifier a provider. Either change must be carried into the Article 13(3)(b) instructions: intended purpose; tested accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity and circumstances affecting them; circumstances under intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse leading to Article 9(2) risks; output-explanation capabilities; performance for specific persons or groups; input-data and dataset specifications; and output-interpretation information. Article 12(2) logging must still capture risk or substantial-modification situations, post-market monitoring and Article 26(5) operation monitoring, and Annex IV points 1 and 2 must record the revised description, design specifications and architecture.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

The answer lists the four conditions in Article 6(3) and ties them to the derogation, confirming that exemption depends on the intended task meeting one of those conditions.
The answer explicitly states that changing capabilities and intended use can change classification if the new purpose satisfies one of the Article 6(3) conditions.
The answer notes the exception for profiling, stating that such systems are always high-risk, which matches the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, third-person regulatory tone without self-reference or hedging; information is structured in coherent prose suitable for compliance use.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted: it is not among the prohibited practices in Article 5(1), and teaching illustration does not make the system high-risk on its own. If the images constitute a "deep fake" within Article 3(60), AI-generated or manipulated image content resembling existing persons or events that would falsely appear authentic, the university, as deployer, must disclose under Article 50(4) that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The lighter regime is not available: Article 50(4)'s attenuated disclosure applies only to evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, and its exemption covers only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, not education.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted, noting it is not prohibited under Article 5(1), which aligns with the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) if the content qualifies as a deep fake, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

The answer states the lighter regime does not apply because educational use is not an 'analogous work' to artistic or fictional content, contradicting criterion 3 which asserts that the lighter regime does apply as an analogous work.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption and notes it does not apply to education, matching the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register; clear structure with logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. The tool is not caught by Article 5(1), so the "policing" framing does not make it prohibited or otherwise high-risk on this evidence. Article 5(1)(d) covers predicting a person's risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits, and expressly excludes systems supporting human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity, here, current-cart and checkout anomalies feeding an optional staff bag check. Article 5(1)(c) is likewise not met: there is no evaluation over a certain period of time yielding a social score producing unrelated-context or disproportionate detrimental treatment.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No', which matches the required verdict and is unambiguous.
The answer does not state or imply that Annex III.6 applies only when used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities; it focuses on Article 5 instead.
The answer does not address that a supermarket's tool is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, which is necessary to satisfy this criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Inappropriate because it references 'Article 5(1)' and 'Article 5(1)(d)' without grounding in the applicable provision (Annex III.6 was the relevant basis in the criteria), and frames analysis around a provision not cited in the criteria, suggesting a misapplication of the regulatory framework; however, the prose is structured and readable.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 apply in full; the sectoral opt-out does not disapply them. Under Article 6(1), the operator's system is high-risk because it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A: machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableway installations, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostic medical devices; Section B: civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle type-approval, general vehicle safety, and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment. Article 43(3) states expressly that the Section 2 requirements apply to such systems and form part of the sectoral assessment. Its final subparagraph allows a manufacturer to use a Section A opt-out from third-party assessment only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all Section 2 requirements, the opt-out is conditional on Section 2 compliance, not a release from it. The supplied evidence carries no text for Article 41(1)(a)(i), (iv). Article 43(1)(a), (d) governs only Annex III point 1 systems and is inapplicable.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, which matches the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that the Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing Article 43(3) and explaining its relevance.
The answer explains that the opt-out is conditional on having applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, which captures the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.
